Between turns, the app sends the model only the text of earlier messages, not earlier tool calls or their results.

Is ommiting previous tool calls/results  a common practice for a llm harness? If not, should we just add the tool calls and results back into the request that we send to the llm model? If so, what are some of the problems that you have been struggling with?
Short answer: no, dropping all earlier tool calls and results isn't the usual default. Yes, I think we should send them again, at least in the printer chat. And to be clear about the last part: I haven't tried this yet, so I haven't hit problems with it. What follows is what I expect from reading the code, not what I ran into.
Is dropping them common practice?
The usual pattern, and what OpenAI's and Anthropic's tool-use docs assume, is to keep the whole transcript: user messages, the assistant's tool calls, the tool results, and the replies. The model's later decisions depend on what earlier tools returned. Mature harnesses do trim, but selectively: they compact or summarize old results when the context grows large, shorten very large outputs, or drop images. Throwing away every tool result at every turn boundary is unusual.
Why this app does it anyway
It looks like a deliberate choice made for the project chat, not an oversight:

* History is rebuilt from the saved chat document as "bounded semantic history": the last 20 messages, text only (`AgentHost.cpp` 1648–1669).
* The project chat sends a fresh, authoritative snapshot of the workspace on every turn. Old tool results there would mostly repeat that snapshot, and could contradict it once the project changed. The code already keeps the app's own notes out of the project chat for exactly that reason (line ~1655).
* Within one turn the app does keep everything. `OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp` 205 says "retain the complete turn input, including... earlier tool results, for each continuation". Results are only lost between turns.

The printer chat has no workspace snapshot (`include_workspace = false`). So the reason for dropping results doesn't apply there, but the cost does: the looked-up printer id disappears before the person says "connect it".
Should we add them back?
For the printer chat, yes. I'd do it with a per-session switch, like the existing `notes_in_context` flag that the printer chat already turns on. The project chat would be untouched, and the change stays in the fork's own agent code.
Problems I'd expect

1. The provider's call ids aren't saved. OpenAI requires each `function_call` to be followed by a `function_call_output` with the same `call_id`. The app stores each tool activity with its arguments and result (`ToolActivity` in `ToolExecution.hpp`), but the provider's `call_id` is described as "opaque outside the service" (`AgentService.hpp:75`) and isn't kept. We'd either save it, or make up ids at replay time. I believe made-up ids work when history is resent in full, which is what `store:false` means, but I haven't verified it.
2. Every call needs an output, including calls that were cancelled, rejected or still pending. A dangling call makes the request invalid. The printer chat already has a result for cancelled calls (`{"state":"cancelled"}` in `PrinterConversation::tool_output`), so this is mostly covered.
3. Stale facts. A connection status from five minutes ago may no longer be true. The model might trust it instead of checking again. That's milder than inventing an id, but worth a prompt test case.
4. Size. Tool results are much bigger than chat text. The printer tools' results are small, but images or big payloads would count against the 20-message window, and a limit would need to count results too.
5. Secrets. The access code must never enter the history. By design it goes straight from the card to the connection and isn't in `printer_connect`'s arguments or result, and the live test already checks that. Replaying results widens where a leak would show up, so that check matters more.
6. The prompt test must copy the change. `run_prompt_tests.py` deliberately copies the text-only history. It would need the same switch, and the connect case should then be measured before and after. I'd expect the made-up ids and the sensitivity to wording to mostly disappear, but that's a prediction until measured.

This one change would also cover the fragile part of your proposed add flow: the model could see its own earlier `printer_identify` call and wouldn't need to repeat it after "Yes, add it".
Did you mix up a lot of things here? I am not following what you are trying to say with the workspace snapshot. Can you rephrase my question so that I can be sure that you understood this correctly, and then try to answer that again, clearly and concisely, with plain English, no jargons.
Yes, I mixed too much in. Here is your question as I understand it:
"When our app sends a new message to the AI, it leaves out the tools the AI used earlier in the chat and what those tools returned. Do other AI apps normally do that? If not, should we just include them? And what goes wrong if we do?"
Do other apps normally leave them out? No. The normal practice is to send the whole conversation every time, including which tools the AI used and what they returned. The AI needs that to remember what it already found out. Apps sometimes shorten very long tool output to save space, but they don't throw it all away.
Why does our app leave them out? My best guess, from the code comments, is that it was designed for the main project chat. There, the app attaches a fresh description of the open project to every message, so old tool output could be out of date and conflict with it. The printer chat attaches no such description, so it simply loses the information, like the printer's id.
Should we include them? Yes, at least in the printer chat. That fixes the "made-up printer id" failure at its root, instead of working around it in the system prompt.
What could go wrong? I haven't tried it yet, so these are what I'd expect, not problems I ran into:

1. Some bookkeeping is missing. Each tool call needs an id that links it to its result. The app saves the calls and results, but not that id, so we'd have to start saving it.
2. Old results can go stale. "The printer is online" may no longer be true ten minutes later. The AI might trust it instead of checking again.
3. Longer requests. More text is sent each time, which costs a bit more. The printer tools' results are small, so this is minor.
4. The access code must never be included. It already never goes through the tools, so this should hold, but it's worth keeping the existing test that checks it.

---
title: Manage tool context
url: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context
description: Choose between tool search, programmatic tool calling, prompt caching, and context editing to manage context bloat.
---

Tool definitions and accumulated `tool_result` blocks consume your context window. Long-running agents with many tools or many turns can exhaust available context before the task is finished. Four approaches address this at different points in the pipeline.

## The four approaches

Each approach targets a different source of context pressure. Pick the one that matches where your tokens are going.

| Approach                  | What it reduces                         | When it fits                                                         | Learn more                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tool search               | Tool definitions loaded upfront         | Large toolsets (20+ tools) where most tools aren't needed every turn | [Tool search tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool)                         |
| Programmatic tool calling | `tool_result` roundtrips                | Chains of tool calls that can execute as a single script             | [Programmatic tool calling](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/programmatic-tool-calling)       |
| Prompt caching            | Token cost of repeated tool definitions | Stable toolsets across many requests                                 | [Tool use with prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-use-with-prompt-caching) |
| Context editing           | Old `tool_result` blocks in history     | Long conversations where early results are no longer relevant        | [Context editing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing)                                   |

### Tool search

Tool search keeps tool definitions out of the context window until Claude asks for them. Instead of sending 50 tool schemas upfront, you send a single `tool_search` tool and let Claude discover the rest on demand. This trades a small amount of latency (one extra turn to look up a tool) for a large reduction in baseline context usage.

### Programmatic tool calling

Programmatic tool calling collapses a sequence of tool calls into a single code block that Claude writes and Anthropic's code execution sandbox runs. Rather than five roundtrips of `tool_use` and `tool_result`, Claude emits one script that calls all five functions from within the sandbox. The intermediate results never enter the conversation history.

### Prompt caching

Prompt caching doesn't reduce the number of tokens in context, but it reduces what you pay for them on subsequent requests. If your tool definitions are stable, cache them once and reuse the cached prefix across thousands of requests. This is the right choice when the toolset is large but fixed.

### Context editing

Context editing removes old `tool_result` blocks from the conversation history once they've served their purpose. A long agent loop might produce hundreds of intermediate results that were useful at the time but are now dead weight. Context editing lets you trim them without restarting the conversation.

## Combining approaches

These approaches compose. A long-running agent might use tool search to keep the toolset lean, prompt caching to amortize the cost of the remaining definitions, and context editing to trim stale results as the conversation grows. Each solves a different part of the problem, so there's no conflict in using them together.

A reasonable starting point for a high-volume agent:

1. Enable prompt caching on your tool definitions from day one. Cache writes carry a 25% markup over base input pricing, which pays back on the second request that hits the cache.
2. Add tool search once your toolset grows past roughly 20 tools or your baseline context usage becomes noticeable.
3. Add context editing once individual conversations start running long enough that early results become irrelevant.
4. Consider programmatic tool calling if you notice repetitive chains of small tool calls that could run as a single batch.

The other agent's answers hold up. I checked every code claim against this worktree and the two API vendors' docs. Everything it stated as fact is accurate, and the things it labeled as guesses are correctly labeled as guesses. Two points need correcting or adding.

**What checks out**

- Between turns the app rebuilds history from the saved chat as role plus text only, capped at the last 20 messages. That is exactly [AgentHost.cpp:1648](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/AgentHost.cpp:1648) through 1669.
- Within one turn the provider keeps the full input, including tool results. The comment is at [OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp:204](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp:204).
- The printer chat turns the workspace off and notes on at [PrinterConversation.cpp:261](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/PrinterConversation.cpp:261). The "notes in context" flag is a real per-session switch the same change could copy.
- The provider's call id is not saved. The saved activity record keeps the tool name, arguments, result, state, and the assistant message it belongs to, but no call id. The host holds the call id only while the turn is live, at [AgentHost.cpp:1757](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/AgentHost.cpp:1757).
- A rejected card is reported back as cancelled, at [PrinterConversation.cpp:361](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/PrinterConversation.cpp:361).
- The prompt test copies the text-only history on purpose. Its own docstring says so. Note that this test exists only on the other branch, at commit 52be072920, not in this worktree.
- Best practice is as the agent described. Anthropic's docs say to keep a running message list and append to it, and treat clearing old tool results as a threshold-based trimming strategy, not the default. OpenAI's guide appends the whole previous output, calls included, to the next input.

**What to correct or add**

1. There is a trap the agent did not mention. Each function call the model returns carries two ids: a `call_id` that links it to its result, and an item `id` that names a server-stored object. With storage off, that item id refers to nothing, and other projects have hit errors by replaying it. So when replaying saved calls, send the call id and omit the item id. Whether a client-made call id is accepted is not documented anywhere I found. Saving the real one is a one-field change, so I would do that rather than test the undocumented case.
2. The printer chat is less blind than the answer implies. The system prompt already lists the printers on the network with their serials, at [printerInstructions.ts:78](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts:78). The app's notes about a verified, added, or cancelled connection already reach the model. And the connect tool accepts the printer's name in place of its id and lists the valid ids when it refuses, at [PrinterConversation.cpp:292](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/PrinterConversation.cpp:292). Replaying tool history still fixes the root cause, but the current failure is narrower than "the information is lost".
3. One small detail: after each tool call the app starts a new assistant message, so a turn with two tool calls is three assistant messages, and all of them count toward the 20-message cap.

**The "why does the app drop them" answer** is honestly marked as a guess, and the code supports only part of it. The comment explains why notes are skipped in the project chat. Nothing in the code states why tool calls and results are dropped, so that remains inference.

**The root cause.** Between turns, AgentHost sends only the messages' text. It sends no function calls and no function_call_outputs. In turn 1 the model calls printer_connection_status and learns `deviceId: FAKE001`, then says "I found one A1 mini". On "Yes, connect it" that result is gone, so a model that calls printer_connect without checking again invents an id (`<from_status>`, `A1 mini`, `<deviceId from printer_connection_status>`) and gets unknown_device. **Rates**, from `tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py` (connect-bambu):
- Shipped prompt: about 64% (32 of 50).
- With a prompt line about the "Printer added" receipt card: 4 of 20.

**Why small prompt edits swing it (ablation, 2026-09-24, 60 to 90 runs per variant):**
- The model almost never looks the printer up again on "connect it" (0-15% of runs).
- A run passes only when its first reply happens to quote the display name "JusPrin Fake A1 mini", which the app accepts as an id: those runs pass about 87% of the time. The rest of the time the model rebuilds an id from the name, e.g. JUSPRIN_FAKE_A1_MINI.
- When the reply doesn't name the printer and the model doesn't look again, the run fails every time (0 of 129).
- Quoting the name is incidental style that any edit shifts: the shipped prompt names it in 83% of runs, neutral unrelated sentences in about 60%, the receipt line in 38%, and the full receipt change in 19%.
